Find Target Sample Sizes for the Accuracy in Standardized Conditions Means Estimation in CRD

Source: R/ss_aipe_crd_es.R
ss_aipe_crd_es.Rd

Finds the number of clusters, the number of individuals per cluster, or both, for a two-condition cluster randomized design (CRD), so that the confidence interval for the standardized difference between the condition means has a desired width or is as narrow as a budget allows. Four of the functions fix one of the two sizes and take a desired width or a budget; the two both functions take a budget and return the sizes that give the narrowest interval, or take a desired width and return the least costly sizes. Each returns a table with the size or sizes found, the cost, and the expected width of the interval where it was computed.

The interval is the likelihood-based confidence interval (Cheung, 2009) computed by the OpenMx package (Boker et al., 2011). See Pornprasertmanit and Schneider (2014) for the method.

Usage

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(
  width,
  cluster_size,
  true_es,
  es_type = 1,
  true_icc,
  pr_treat,
  true_R2_between = 0,
  true_R2_within = 0,
  n_covariates = 0,
  assurance = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  G = 1000,
  true_icc_covariate = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1,
  cluster_cost = NULL,
  individual_cost = NULL,
  diff_size = NULL
)

Arguments

width

The desired width of the confidence interval of the standardized difference between the condition means

cluster_size

The number of individuals in each cluster: a single whole number of at least 2

true_es

The population effect size the interval is planned for (on the scale chosen by es_type): a single finite number, such as 0.5. It is required wherever a width is computed, because the width is read from data simulated at that value: in the four planners that take or return a width, and in the two planners that fix a size and a budget when G is supplied. A call that asks for a width without it is refused with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid that names what is missing

es_type

The type of effect size. There are only three possible options: 0 = the effect size using total standard deviation, 1 = the effect size using the individual-level standard deviation (level 1), 2 = the effect size using the cluster-level standard deviation (level 2)

true_icc

The population intraclass correlation of the dependent variable (a planning value): a single number in [0, 1), and above 0 with es_type = 2. At 1 no variance lies within clusters, and the model fitted to each simulated data set has no within-cluster variance to estimate; with es_type = 2 the effect is in units of the between-cluster standard deviation, which an intraclass correlation of 0 makes 0

pr_treat

The proportion of treatment clusters: a single number strictly between 0 and 1

true_R2_between

The population proportion of the between-level variance that the covariate explains (a planning value in [0, 1), used when n_covariates = 1; the default is 0 in all six functions). It must be 0 when n_covariates = 0

true_R2_within

The population proportion of the within-level variance that the covariate explains (a planning value in [0, 1), used when n_covariates = 1; the default is 0 in all six functions)

n_covariates

The number of covariates at the cluster (between) level, not counting the treatment indicator: 0 (the default, the treatment indicator alone) or 1. A larger value is refused. It is not p, the total number of predictors, which here is p = n_covariates + 1.

assurance

The assurance: the probability, over repeated studies of the design, that the study gives a confidence interval and that the interval is no wider than the width planned (e.g., .80, .90, .95). With NULL (the default) the plan is for the expected width instead. A simulated data set whose interval cannot be formed counts as one whose interval is wider than any width (see the section on simulated data sets without a usable interval)

conf_level

The desired level of confidence for the confidence interval

G

The number of replications used in the a priori Monte Carlo simulation: a single whole number from 1 to 999,999 (default 1000 in the four planners that need a simulation). Each simulated data set takes its own seed, drawn without replacement from the whole numbers 1 to 999,999, so no more can be simulated. Anything else (a fractional number, 0, a negative number, a number above 999,999, NA, a character string, or more than one value) is refused with an error of class dmar_count_invalid before any simulation starts. In the two planners that fix a size and a budget the default is NULL, which skips the simulation: the size the budget buys is returned without an expected width. Supplying G there asks for the expected width, which also needs pr_treat, true_icc, and true_es; a call with G and without any of them is refused, with a message that names the ones missing, in place of a table without the width that was asked for.

true_icc_covariate

The population intraclass correlation of the covariate (a planning value, used when n_covariates = 1; when it is NULL the value of true_icc is used). If true_icc_covariate = 0, the covariate varies within clusters only. If true_icc_covariate = 1, the covariate varies between clusters only

seed

An optional integer seed for the a priori Monte Carlo simulation. The default NULL draws the seeds of the simulated data sets from the current random number stream, which advances that stream, so repeated calls reflect the sampling variability of the simulation. An integer makes the result reproducible: the seed is set for the call only, and the caller's random number state is restored when the function returns

ncpus

The number of processes over which the G simulated data sets are spread, the name this count has in the bootstrap functions of the package (reliability_omega and its relatives). The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger whole number uses forked workers or, on Windows, which cannot fork, a socket cluster. Each simulated data set has its own seed, drawn before any is run, so a given seed returns the same result whatever ncpus is. A socket cluster is stopped when the function exits, whether it returns, stops with an error, or is interrupted.

cluster_cost

The cost of adding one cluster, whatever the number of individuals in it: a single finite number of 0 or more. Where the costs choose the design (the two budget planners that fix a size and the two both planners), cluster_cost and individual_cost cannot both be 0

individual_cost

The cost of adding one individual to a cluster: a single finite number of 0 or more, and positive where the costs choose the cluster size (ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_budget and the two both planners)

diff_size

Difference cluster size specification. The differences in cluster sizes can be specified in two ways, and the specified vector is recycled across the clusters. First, users may specify differences as integers, which can be negative or positive; the resulting cluster sizes add the specified values to the estimated cluster size. For example, if the cluster size is 25, the number of clusters is 10, and diff_size = c(-1, 0, 1), the cluster sizes will be 24, 25, 26, 24, 25, 26, 24, 25, 26, and 24. Second, users may specify multipliers of the cluster size as positive decimals; at least one value must be non-integer, which is what selects the multiplicative form. The resulting cluster sizes multiply the estimated cluster size by the specified values and round to the nearest integer. For example, if the cluster size is 25, the number of clusters is 10, and diff_size = c(0.8, 1, 1.2), the cluster sizes will be 20, 25, 30, 20, 25, 30, 20, 25, 30, and 20. In either form a resulting cluster size below 1 is set to 1. If NULL, the cluster size is equal across clusters

n_clusters

The number of clusters: a single whole number of at least 3 + n_covariates, which with pr_treat puts a cluster in each condition

budget

The amount available for the study, in the units of cluster_cost and individual_cost: a single finite number of 0 or more

Value

The ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width and ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget functions provide the number of clusters. The ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width and ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_budget functions provide the cluster size. The ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_budget and ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_width provide the number of clusters and the cluster size, respectively.

Each returns a table with the columns term and value. The rows, where they apply, are necessary_n_clusters (the number of clusters, where it is solved for), necessary_cluster_size (the number of individuals in each cluster, where it is solved for; with diff_size the cluster sizes and their frequencies are printed ahead of the table instead), width (the desired width, in the functions that plan from one), the width of the interval for the standardized effect size chosen by es_type, and budget (the cost of the design, when the two costs are supplied). Without assurance the width row is expected_width, the mean width of the interval over the G simulated data sets. With assurance it is assured_width, the width that the interval does not exceed with the requested probability, followed by the row assurance that echoes that probability.

A size that was given is an argument of the call and is not repeated in the table: only a size the function solved for has a row, and its name begins with necessary_. tidy and glance report the planned size as estimate (the number of clusters where it was solved for, otherwise the cluster size) and the desired width as width, which is NA for a plan made from a budget; glance() carries expected_width or assured_width as a column of that name.

A table whose width was simulated carries the record of the simulation of the design reported in its attribute simulation, a list read with attr(x, "simulation"): attempted (G), returned (the data sets with a usable interval), failed (those without one), denominator (the number of data sets the width row is taken over: returned for expected_width, attempted for assured_width), failure_reasons (the data sets without a usable interval by reason, a named integer vector: "fit_error", "optimizer_status_<code>", "limit_not_found", "limit_status_<code>", "limit_not_finite", "limits_not_ordered"), failure_messages (for a fit that stopped with an error, the first error message, named by reason), width (the width reported), width_mc_ci (the Monte Carlo interval of that width at conf_level, which describes the error of the simulation only: the mean plus and minus the normal quantile times its standard error, or for the assured width the interval of two order statistics of the G widths), n_clusters and cluster_size (the design), and search, the totals over every design the call simulated (n_designs, attempted, returned, failed, failure_reasons, failure_messages) and the warnings the fits gave (warnings, one element per kind, with its class, first message, all its messages, and n, the number of data sets that gave it). The line "Replications" beneath the printed table gives G, and the three counts when a data set gave no usable interval.

Details

Here are the functions' descriptions:

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width

Find the number of clusters given a specified width of the confidence interval and the cluster size

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width

Find the cluster size given a specified width of the confidence interval and the number of clusters

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget

Find the number of clusters given a budget and the cluster size

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_budget

Find the cluster size given a budget and the number of clusters

ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_budget

Find the sample size combinations (the number of clusters and that cluster size) providing the narrowest confidence interval given the fixed budget

ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_width

Find the sample size combinations (the number of clusters and that cluster size) providing the lowest cost given the specified width of the confidence interval

Every answer that targets a width, and the expected width a budget planner reports when G and the population values are supplied, rests on an a priori Monte Carlo simulation: a candidate design is evaluated by generating G data sets and reading the likelihood-based confidence interval on the standardized effect size from OpenMx. The planners whose answer needs one such evaluation, or a handful, run in about a second at a small G and are the ones shown in the examples. The two that search over the number of clusters, ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width at a fixed cluster size and ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_width, which repeats that search across candidate cluster sizes and keeps the least costly combination that reaches the width, evaluate many candidates in turn and run for minutes at the default G = 1000, so they are not among the examples. A call such as ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.3, cluster_size = 20, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5, G = 1000, seed = 113) returns the number of clusters of 20 individuals that brings the expected width of the interval on the individual-level standardized effect size to 0.3, and ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_width(width = 0.5, cluster_cost = 5, individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5, G = 1000, seed = 113) returns the least costly pairing of clusters and cluster size at those costs that reaches a width of 0.5. Both accept diff_size for unequal cluster sizes, in which case the simulated data sets carry the unequal sizes and the confidence interval comes from a multiple-group model.

The width of a simulated interval is its upper limit minus its lower limit.

Simulated data sets without a usable interval

Each simulated data set is fitted with OpenMx, and its interval is used only when the fit and the search for each limit succeeded: the optimizer status code of the fit and of each limit's search is 0 or 1 (the codes that OpenMx's as.statusCode() describes as "OK" and "OK/green", optimization succeeded; with a code such as 5, a Hessian that does not appear to be convex, or 6, a solution that does not meet the first-order optimality conditions, the fit may not be at the maximum the interval is measured from, and that help page advises against trusting it), OpenMx's diagnostic for each limit is "success", and the two limits are finite and bracket the estimate. A data set that fails any of these, or whose fit stops with an error, gives no usable interval. How often that happens depends on the design. With OpenMx 2.22.11 and a standardized effect of 0.5 (the intraclass correlation in parentheses), the share of 1000 simulated data sets without a usable interval, with its Monte Carlo standard error, was 0 with 20 clusters of 10 (0.2) and es_type = 1, 0.002 (0.0014) with six clusters of 5 (0.1), 0 with ten clusters of 2 (0.01), 0 with eight clusters of 4 (0.1) and es_type = 0, 0.415 (0.016) with six clusters of two to four individuals (0.05), and 0.208 (0.013) with 20 clusters of 10 (0.2) and es_type = 2; a second run of 400 data sets gave 0.378 (0.024) and 0.237 (0.021) for the last two. These are single runs, and other versions of OpenMx can give other shares. With the unequal clusters 412 of the 415 failed fits ended with status 5 or 6, and in 200 further data sets each of the 86 such fits had estimated the between-cluster variance below 0. The effect of es_type = 2 is divided by the between-cluster standard deviation, which can be near 0: for some data sets the likelihood does not fall far enough on one side for a finite limit to exist, for others OpenMx's search does not reach a limit that exists, and some of the intervals it does find are very wide (with 20 clusters of 10, the usable intervals of 300 data sets had a median width of 2.1, 10 of 242 were wider than 10, and 2 wider than 100), so that their mean rests on a few data sets.

Without assurance, the expected width is the mean width over the data sets that gave a usable interval, so it describes studies in which the interval could be formed. With assurance, a data set without a usable interval counts as one whose interval is wider than any width, and the assured width is the assurance quantile of the widths of all G data sets; the assurance is then the probability that a study gives an interval and that the interval is no wider than the assured width. When more than about 1 - assurance of the data sets give no usable interval, no width is reached with that probability.

When some of the data sets simulated at the design reported gave no usable interval, a warning of class dmar_replications_without_interval (with scope "design") gives their number, the reasons, and the number of data sets the width is taken over. When every data set at the design reported gave an interval but some at other designs the search simulated did not, a warning of the same class (with scope "search") gives the totals of the search, since those data sets bear on where it stopped. When none gave one, or the assurance cannot be reached, the function stops with an error of class dmar_computation_failed that carries the counts (attempted, returned, failed, failure_reasons), and no table is returned. Inside a search such a design counts as one whose width does not meet the target. For a fit that stopped with an error, the warning and the error give the first error message, which names the cause when every data set fails for one reason.

A warning that a fit gives is not discarded: each kind of warning is given once when the function exits, as a warning of class dmar_result_qualified that says how many simulated data sets gave it and carries its own class as warning_class. Warnings of one class whose messages differ only in their numbers count as one kind; the first message is shown, and all of them are in the field messages. The warning OpenMx gives for an optimizer status other than 0 is not passed on: a fit of status 1 is used, as OpenMx's help describes it, and any other status is counted as the reason the data set has no usable interval.

The searches

The planners that search for a size start from the size the unstandardized difference between the condition means needs (the cluster size search with es_type = 1 can start lower; see below), and each size they try is a simulation of G data sets. A width meets the target when it is no larger than the target. From a start whose width meets the target, the search steps down one cluster or one individual at a time to the smallest size that still meets it. From a start whose width is above the target, the search steps up 1, 3, 7, 15, and so on, past the start until the width meets the target, and then halves the gap between the last size that did not meet it and the first that did until the two are adjacent. When the simulated width falls as the size grows, this gives the smallest size that meets the target, the size that stepping up one at a time gives, with far fewer sizes simulated. With a small G the simulated width can rise and fall from one size to the next, and then the two can stop at different sizes near the target. The same holds when designs without a finite width (see below) lie among designs with one, as can happen near the share of failed data sets an assurance allows: the search returns a size that meets the target next to one that does not, which need not be the smallest size that meets it.

The search for the number of clusters has no upper bound, since the width falls toward 0 as clusters are added wherever it is finite. A design at which no simulated data set gives a usable interval, or at which too few do for the assurance, has no finite width; after such a design the next size tried is at least twice as large, and three such designs in a row stop the search with an error of class dmar_computation_failed, with reason "no_finite_width", that gives the sizes, the counts, and the reasons.

With a fixed number of clusters the width levels off as the clusters grow, because the clusters themselves vary, so a target can be out of reach at any cluster size. For es_type = 1 with no covariate at the cluster level, the value it levels off at is known: as every cluster grows, the within-cluster standard deviation becomes known and the cluster means exact, and the likelihood-based interval for the difference between K cluster means with a common unknown variance has a width whose mean (or, with assurance, whose quantile) has a closed form. A target at or below that value is refused before anything is simulated, with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid, reason "width_not_reachable", that gives it as width_limit; a target above it is reached by some cluster size. There the search starts from the smaller of two sizes: the size the unstandardized difference needs, and the size at which the expected width (or its quantile) with the within-cluster standard deviation known falls below the target. That width is the value the width levels off at, with the variance of a cluster mean at the size in place of the between-cluster variance. The unstandardized difference uses the t quantile on K - 2 degrees of freedom, and with few clusters it needs far more: with 10 clusters and an intraclass correlation of .2 it needs 1,875 individuals per cluster for a target of 1.46, where about 10 reach it with true_es = 0.5 (the size the unstandardized difference needs does not depend on the effect, but the size that reaches the target grows with it). With equal cluster sizes, no covariate, and no assurance, the start is a lower bound on the cluster size the target needs (the second of the two sizes uses true_R2_within only with a covariate, since the simulated data use it only then). The likelihood-based interval contains the interval computed with the within-cluster standard deviation fixed at its maximum likelihood estimate, whose expected width is the width with the deviation known times the mean of the ratio of the deviation to its estimate, which exceeds 1; so at every smaller cluster size the expected width is above the target. With es_type = 0 or 2, or with a covariate at the cluster level, the search starts from the size the unstandardized difference needs, and only when that is at most 100,000 individuals per cluster. The cluster size search simulates cluster sizes up to 100 above the size the unstandardized difference needs (above its own start when that size is beyond 100,000) and never above 500, since the model has one variable per individual of a cluster and a fit takes far longer as the clusters grow; a search that would start above 500 individuals per cluster is refused before anything is simulated, with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid, reason "cluster_size_beyond_reach", that gives the start as start and, as lower_bound, whether it is a lower bound in the sense just given; the message calls it one only then. A width still above the target there stops it with an error of class dmar_computation_failed, reason "width_not_reached", that gives the sizes searched and the narrowest width found with its Monte Carlo interval. The message says whether a larger cluster size reaches the target (where the value the width levels off at is known) or that this was not determined, and suggests a larger G only when the target lies within that Monte Carlo interval.

The number of clusters the unstandardized difference needs, from which the search over the number of clusters starts, is at least ceiling(2 / min(pr_treat, 1 - pr_treat)) + n_covariates, which puts two clusters in each condition (see ss_aipe_crd), and the search steps down no further than the last design with two clusters in each condition. A start beyond 1,000,000 clusters, the most the unstandardized search considers, is refused before anything is simulated, with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid, reason "n_clusters_beyond_reach". The planners that search over both sizes start from the plan of the unstandardized difference, which keeps the same floor, and do not simulate a number of clusters at which the budget does not buy clusters of 2.

A call simulates at most 500 designs; the two planners that search over both sizes share that bound among the searches they run, and three neighboring designs with no finite width stop ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_budget. A call that reaches the bound stops with an error of class dmar_computation_failed, reason "search_budget", that gives the totals. These bounds limit the computation; none of them is a statistical rule.

Refused calls

The design arguments, the costs, and the budget are checked before anything is simulated, as in ss_aipe_crd (see its section on refused calls): n_covariates a whole number of 0 or more (and here at most 1), cluster_size a whole number of at least 2, n_clusters a whole number of at least 3 + n_covariates that puts a cluster in each condition, pr_treat strictly between 0 and 1, true_R2_between and true_R2_within in [0, 1), true_R2_between 0 when n_covariates = 0 (reason "R2_between_without_covariates"), diff_size NULL or a vector of one or more finite numbers, and each cost and the budget a single finite number of 0 or more. Wherever a width is simulated (always in the four planners that take a width or search over both sizes, and with G in the other two), es_type must be 0, 1, or 2, true_icc as described under its argument, and, with a covariate, true_icc_covariate in [0, 1]. Costs that are both 0 are refused where they choose the design (reason "costs_all_zero"), and individual_cost = 0 where they choose the cluster size (reason "individual_cost_zero"). A budget that does not buy the smallest design a planner can return is refused with reason "budget_infeasible" and the cost of that design as min_cost (with G, the smallest design with a cluster in each condition and a degree of freedom), and a budget whose design leaves a condition without a cluster, when its width is asked for, with reason "arm_without_clusters". A fixed n_clusters that leaves a condition without a cluster is refused with the same reason where a width is simulated: always in ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width, and in ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_budget only with G, since without it pr_treat is not used. Each of these has class dmar_argument_invalid. assurance must be NULL or a single number strictly between 0 and 1 in all six planners (class dmar_assurance_invalid), and the three planners that take a width refuse one that is not a single positive number. ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width refuses, with reason "cluster_size_beyond_reach" and start = Inf, a search whose start, the cluster size the unstandardized difference needs, is beyond 100,000.

References

Boker, S. M., Neale, M. C., Maes, H. H., Wilde, M., Spiegel, M., Brick, T. R., ... Fox, J. (2011). OpenMx: An open source extended structural equation modeling framework. Psychometrika, 76(2), 306–317. doi:10.1007/s11336-010-9200-6

Cheung, M. W.-L. (2009). Constructing approximate confidence intervals for parameters with structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling, 16(2), 267–294. doi:10.1080/10705510902751291

Pornprasertmanit, S., & Schneider, W. J. (2010). Efficient sample size for power and desired accuracy in Cohen's d estimation in two-group cluster randomized design (Master Thesis). Illinois State University, Normal, IL.

Pornprasertmanit, S., & Schneider, W. J. (2014). Accuracy in parameter estimation in cluster randomized designs. Psychological Methods, 19(3), 356–379. doi:10.1037/a0037036

See also

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Two of these planners answer a question the budget alone settles. Given
# what it costs to open a cluster and what it costs to collect one more
# individual, the first reports how many clusters a budget buys at a fixed
# cluster size and the second reports how large each cluster can be at a
# fixed number of clusters. Clusters cost nothing to open here and each
# individual costs 1, so the budget buys 1000 individuals and the only
# question is how to arrange them.
ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,
  cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1)
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 50   
#>  budget               1000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, n_clusters = 200,
  cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1)
#>  term                   value
#>  necessary_cluster_size 5    
#>  budget                 1000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The interval width these planners can report, and every answer that
# targets a width, rests on an a priori Monte Carlo simulation: a candidate
# design is evaluated by generating G data sets and reading the
# likelihood-based confidence interval on the standardized effect size from
# OpenMx. The calls below use G = 2 so that the page runs quickly; a
# reported plan deserves the default G = 1000. Each call describes a
# population standardized effect size of 0.5, with es_type = 1 putting that
# effect size in individual-level standard deviation units and a quarter of
# the outcome variance lying between clusters.

# Supplying G and the population values to a budget planner adds the
# expected width of the interval the affordable design buys.
ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,
  cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25,
  pr_treat = 0.5, G = 2, seed = 113)
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 50   
#>  expected_width       0.673
#>  budget               1000 
#> 
#> Replications: 2
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Cluster size needed for a target width, given the number of clusters.
# With 250 clusters the planner settles on the smallest cluster size it
# will consider, two individuals per cluster, and the expected width still
# comes in under the target: for a contrast between conditions that are
# assigned at the cluster level, precision is bought with clusters rather
# than with what happens inside them.
ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 0.5, n_clusters = 250,
  true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5, G = 2,
  seed = 113)
#>  term                   value
#>  necessary_cluster_size 2    
#>  width                  0.500
#>  expected_width         0.473
#> 
#> Replications: 2
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Once recruiting a cluster costs 5, the number of clusters and the cluster
# size trade off against each other, and this planner searches the
# combinations the budget allows for the narrowest expected interval.
ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_cost = 5,
  individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5,
  G = 2, seed = 113)
#>  term                   value
#>  necessary_n_clusters   111  
#>  necessary_cluster_size 4    
#>  expected_width         0.593
#>  budget                 999  
#> 
#> Replications: 2
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Unequal cluster sizes. Every planner accepts diff_size, which gives each
# cluster's deviation from cluster_size as an integer offset or as a
# multiplicative factor, recycled across the clusters; the planner prints
# the resulting cluster sizes and their frequencies ahead of its table.
# The budget planner shows both forms here.
ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,
  cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1, diff_size = c(-2, 1, 0, 2, -1, 3, -3, 0, 0))
#>   cluster_size freq
#> 1           17    5
#> 2           18    6
#> 3           19    6
#> 4           20   16
#> 5           21    6
#> 6           22    6
#> 7           23    5
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 50   
#>  budget               1000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,
  cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1,
  diff_size = c(0.6, 1.2, 0.8, 1.4, 1, 1, 1.1, 0.9))
#>   cluster_size freq
#> 1           12    7
#> 2           16    6
#> 3           18    6
#> 4           20   12
#> 5           22    6
#> 6           24    7
#> 7           28    6
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 50   
#>  budget               996  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
